lecture_context.lecture_title: What’s Going On Inside My Model?

unit.name: Training telemetry, loss curves, and scaling laws
unit.description: Explains how frontier labs use loss curves, telemetry, and scaling laws to detect instability and decide whether to invest in compute, data, or model capacity.
unit.summary: The training-diagnostics section starts with smooth training and validation loss curves as a basic health check; sudden jumps, plateaus, exploding gradients, vanishing gradients, or corrupted batches can appear through these signals [ts=4704s] [ts=4715s] [ts=4743s]. The instructor broadens telemetry to gradient norms, learning-rate schedules, checkpoint tracking, and hardware efficiency, noting that full dashboards are rarely published because they reveal IP [ts=4781s] [ts=4806s]. Scaling laws are presented as public evidence for relating performance to model size, compute, and data set size [ts=4842s] [ts=4860s]. The Chinchilla example is used to explain undertraining: GPT-3 is described as underutilized because a smaller 70B-parameter Chinchilla model could outperform the 175B-parameter GPT-3 when trained more compute-optimally [ts=4877s] [ts=4912s] [ts=4978s].

key_points.text: Smooth training and validation loss curves are a first signal that a model is training normally.
Sudden jumps in loss can indicate corrupted batches, bugs, exploding gradients, or vanishing gradients.
Training telemetry includes gradient norms, learning-rate schedules, and hardware-efficiency metrics.
Scaling laws relate model performance to capacity, compute, and data-set size.
Chinchilla is used as an example that a smaller model trained longer can outperform a larger undertrained one.
Scaling laws guide expensive decisions about whether to train longer, collect more data, or increase model capacity.

kp_catalog.name: Pretraining scaling and compute-data tradeoffs
kp_catalog.description: Large-scale pretraining quality depends jointly on model size, training data, and compute budget, with capabilities improving as those resources scale. This scaling view also appears in vision-language systems such as CLIP, where larger models and more image-text data improve performance.
